title: Equanimity
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The main teaching of the Soto Zen dharma talk emphasizes the importance of integrating different aspects of practice to cultivate true awakening. This involves exploring various qualities of mind, such as mindfulness, discernment, energy, joy, calm, concentration, and wisdom, which are not something that can be forced or achieved, but rather involve a dynamic process of inclining the mind towards awareness, acceptance, and accuracy. By working with attention and cultivating these qualities, individuals can develop a more accurate understanding of themselves and the world around them, leading to greater stability, calmness, and presence in life.

sentences.text: Well, I was really enjoying tonight how our somewhat elaborate structure just creates so many opportunities to train and to try these different jobs.
So I just want to thank everybody who's trying different roles in the zendo.
You would think it's just meditation and then frills, but I think it's really designed to be a very integrated and complete system.

Zazen is in the center of the mandala of practice, but as we're ready and comfortable to start doing things like ringing the bells and leading the chanting and organizing the zendo and being a teacher, just taking up these different roles, see what you learn.
Because you always learn something, right?
And we're always moving through different roles in life, so it's a good way to practice.
I always enjoy pointing out that it's so valuable because we take it so seriously and because it's totally meaningless.
Who really cares if we sit down the exact right way?
It appears that I did.

It just gives us a wonderfully, we hope, safe container, or maybe just dangerous enough to be effective, to study our mind, to study our tendencies, to study how things go for us, to study so many things, right?
Perfectionism is an obvious first target.
Bam!
Knock that one right over.
Hit it as many times as we need to, until you can't hold it up anymore, this target.
You're perfect.
I'm perfect.
I'm perfect.
I'm perfect.
Oh!
Oh, it's okay.

So I thought we would attempt to finish our series of talks on the seven factors of awakening, and I wanted to make a few announcements about the future and other related or unrelated events that are on my mind.
Tonight we'll talk about the seventh and last factor of the seven factors of awakening that were recommended by the Buddha.
And then we'll start into a wonderful series of talks and study on the Zen precepts, the ethical foundation of Zen.
Interestingly enough, these Zen precepts, these ethical guidelines, are also the basis of all of our ordination and empowerment ceremonies.

You would think it would be a sort of preparation, like you would do some ethical work to prepare yourself, but then you would meditate really hard until you had special powers or something, and then you would get empowered or ordained or something like that.
But actually, these magical powers of Soto Zen are paying attention.
Being alive and awake in the middle of our life, being ethical and kind as best we can, and finding out there's always more.

What's fun is that we're going to do a series of talks and study meetings about the precepts on Wednesday night, and we're going to include, I think, pretty much all of the Sangha leaders who are empowered to give talks.
So I'll give some of the talks, and other people will give talks.
I just put the schedule out, and people are really game, and they signed up within hours, and thank goodness, because I was a little behind.
So we'll have talks from John and Edie and Bob and Talus so far, and myself.
Part of the design, which I hope works out for everybody schedule-wise, is that in the talk period there's not much time for discussion, just the way the evening is designed.
We want to have time for meditation and ceremony, so there's a talk and not much time for discussion.
But then on the subsequent Wednesday, you can come early.
You can come at six o'clock, and if the stars are aligned, the teacher who gave the talk the previous week will be there to discuss it.
See?
Isn't that sneaky?
So John gives a talk on intoxicants, that's his plan, sometime in May, I forget when, and then hopefully the next week he'll be able to come early.
Well, maybe not in your case, because you're working, but we'll figure it out.
Okay.
He'll come early the next week, and you'll be able to continue the conversation having thought about it for a week.
That's good, huh?
Or if you missed the talk, you can listen to it online.
We'll try to be diligent about getting them right online, and you can then go to the discussion and not feel like you missed anything.
So that's one thing that's going on.

Connected to that somehow, we want to not only consider our personal conduct and our personal dedication to waking up to what we're doing in our life, but we also want to consider a little more carefully our collective conduct.
Most centers like this have ethical guidelines and guidelines for conduct, and we've been working on it slowly and have just gotten around to it.

So we're going to try to somehow weave the process of creating our process and procedure and guidelines for how we're going to conduct ourselves and how we're going to communicate about it in our sangha life into this study.
Somehow it's going to work out.
We set aside a few nights to be nights of just conversation about that, but hopefully a conversation really informed by our study, not just whatever pops into our mind first.
So that's the plan for the rest of the spring.
Then I want to mention a little about summer.
Bob and I are working on getting the sequence of events for the wilderness hiking program of Red Cedars Inn community.
I got it initially sketched out on the website, but Bob probably will change it all around.
We're working on it and we'll be out there.
So just have that in mind, that as summer approaches, we can bring our practice out onto the trails of Whatcom County and Washington and Oregon even, it turns out, this year.
Go to Oregon.
There's day hikes and a short stroll into a beautiful old growth that doesn't require as much fitness.
There's a three-day backpack and a 14-day backpack, yeah, on the schedule, and another day hike.
So just know that's going on.
It will be gradually elucidated, but it's pretty much late July, August, September.
So just to know, a lot of things we do.
And then the last thing, this is not our Sangha, but it just popped into my mind as I was doing the service.
I was really somehow feeling the presence of my friend Kokyo Henkel, who is a priest in California.
He's my exact same age, and we were at Tassajara Monastery together in 1993, both having recently arrived there.
I left to come to Bellingham and have marriages and kids and lay sanghas together with you.
But Kokyo stayed.
Kokyo Henkel stayed at Tassajara and was resident there for, I think, 16 years.
He left just recently.
So yeah, just like 16 years behind me.
Kokyo is a teacher of the Santa Cruz Zen Center, where our dear Sangha mate Chris Burkhart is right now.
I just saw on Facebook that he's organizing a pilgrimage to India next January.
So that's why I'm mentioning Kokyo Henkel.
He's a very low-to-the-ground guy, so this would be the coolest low...
I mean, you have to be willing to rough it a little bit.
This would be the neatest, most practice-oriented, low-to-the-ground, somewhat lower budget India Buddhist pilgrimage you can imagine.
I really hope I can go.
I haven't even talked to Janet about it, but this is a glimmer of hope.
But if I don't go, maybe one of you can go in my place.
And...
**Participant:** What time of the year is he coming back?
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** January.
Most of January.
Three weeks in January, which is a good time to go to India, as I understand it.
If he's got a thing on Facebook, I can hook you up with Kokyo.
If you want to see where the Buddha was born, and lived and taught and died.
So, a few upcoming events.
Another upcoming event in the summer, exact date almost worked out, almost worked out, is that our dear sangha mate here, Dean Norton, will ordain as a priest.
So we can come to her ordination, and it'll be like a half-day retreat, so we'll get to do zazen with her and sit in emptiness with her as she does this big thing that also doesn't mean anything.
That's good.
Luckily, yeah, thank goodness.
If it meant something, we'd be really in trouble.
Okay, so, a few announcements.
The Buddha recommended that we cultivate seven qualities of mind so that we can really be awake, be happy in a way that's not contingent on conditions, intrinsically content and happy.
So, to review briefly these seven qualities, and we'll try to knock off the last one tonight.
But before we even do that, think about this idea that there are some qualities of mind that we're supposed to develop and generate or uncover or nurture.
There seems to be a dynamic tension there in terms of, well, how would we do that?
Can we make something happen in our head?
Many of our attempts have failed, right?
Make something happen in our mind.

Or is it more like attending to the conditions of our life to increase the chances that these qualities will just bubble forth spontaneously or effervescently, which we have a bit of a cultural bias around, I think?
I think we think that positive emotional states should just arise spontaneously.
You're a faker, right, if you generate them.
Or maybe it's a little bit of all three.
One teacher I've studied says the idea is to incline the mind, to incline the mind in the direction of these qualities.
The idea is that we have a little bit of an orienting power over the mind.
We can give it a little nudge.
I was thinking about the etymology of the word attention, since this is working with attention.
It comes from the verb to attend, which in Latin is attendere, something like that.
That literally means to bend the mind.
We can shape the mind a little bit.
We can't control it, but maybe we can bend it or orient it a little bit, working with our attention.
And maybe it's easier for us to see the working of attention when we look at our sensing of the outside world.
We can notice whether we're just paying attention to one thing or the attention is skipping all around.
Then we can start to develop the ability to be aware of what we're aware of at any given moment, and to start to look at that inside the mind as well, which meditation, of course, helps with.
So we can look at patterns and movement.
What are we doing to practice our practice of just being mindful and awake and aware?

Just remember that there's a whole process of mind going on all the time, and that we tend to pay attention to the endpoint of a very complicated, fast-running process that's drawing conclusions and figuring things out.
We all think we know who we are and who all these other people are and what they should have done and so on.
So mindfulness and attention, and these seven factors, are all about taking up this interesting and curious project of peeling back the layers of mind and wondering, well, how does it actually work?
What actually happens as we interface with experience?
It's also to bring forward what I'm now calling the three As.
I'm starting to think of acronyms, because I'm teaching all these mindfulness classes, and I think it actually is helpful.
I've always hated acronyms, but now that I'm teaching them, they must be good.
So the three As are awareness, acceptance, and accuracy.
Are we aware of what's happening in mind?
Can we accept that whatever is here is actually here?
And can we be a little more accurate about what's being perceived, what's being felt, what's being thought?
Of course, we're never going to be good at this.
It's always going to be a little bit distorted, a little bit muddled.
So this is taking up a vow, or taking up an intention, with the full realization that we're going to be imperfect at this.
So the perfectionism is out.
Interestingly, I've taught this a few times, and the only reaction I've gotten is to this word accuracy.
It sounds dissonant a little bit to some people.
One person was just thrilled.
He knew he was in the right place.
This was not some woo woo wishy washy new agey deal.
You guys are accurate.
That's excellent for me.
And someone else said, "That is such a trap.
You're telling me to be accurate?
I know that I can't do that."
So I'm keeping it, because I think I'm hearing that it's useful to people to reflect on what's accurate, what's clear.
Like we say, clarity.
What's clear, what's accurate, what's actually happening.
This is not a passive kind of acceptance, "oh well, I guess that's what's going on," but a very curious and active investigation.
What's actually happening in mind?
So the seven factors start with mindfulness, just this remembering that we have this possibility of working with mind, and inclining the mind towards awareness of the present.
Then the second factor is discernment or investigation.

Once we can incline the mind towards the present and be curious about the three As, be curious about what we're aware of and what's actually happening, then we can get curious about, well, what really is happening?
Like, "Did I do that?
Wow, how interesting."
As we incline the mind towards the present and towards what's happening, then we can investigate, we can inquire.
That's the second factor: investigation or inquiry.

Once we start investigating and we see how interesting it actually is, at times a little disheartening and a little bit upsetting to open up the cover and look inside the mind, then what arises next is some energy and some motivation and some diligence.
On the list I used the word diligence; I think it's the third factor of awakening.
There's a way that these incline each other in a very organic way, but we have to keep inclining the mind in that direction.
Now it's happening.
Once we have a little energy and a little diligence, we're putting something into our practice.
You have to put something in to get something out.
Then what arises next in the scheme is joy.
Surprise.
A warm interest.
A sense of humor.
We need that.
This joy is a very warm, energized joy, not like "ha ha ha, isn't this great," but we're alive.
Just the wonder of being alive.
It's that kind of joy.

And actually seeing that it's possible to work with some of these deep patterns and qualities of mind, that it actually is possible to explore and influence them a little bit and accept the things that seem to be so intransigent.
So some joy arises.
But then we quickly see that that joy is a little bit unstable.
It's like, whoa!
Then we need to calm down.
Or maybe naturally the energy releases a little bit.
We see that too much of a warm energized joy can create a bit of a [unclear: "scream"] between us and the world too, that it's a little too much.
So then calm is the next factor, the next factor that we can incline the mind towards.
Okay, I'm going to do what I need to do internally, externally to just calm down a little bit.
Ah, breath is so helpful here.
And just remembering this possibility of calm can all by itself shift the situation sometimes on a good day.
None of this is always or ever.
Suzuki Roshi said the true nature of Buddhism is not always so.
So all of these things are not always so.
Once we're calmed down a little bit, then the mind gets a little more stable, and so we have samadhi or concentration.
We spoke about that last week.
I was able to circle back and look up the etymology of the Sanskrit word samadhi.
It means to gather and to place.
Sam means to gather and [unclear: "dra or t"] means to place.
So we gather up our concentration, or ability to be clear and steady, and we place it somewhere.
We might place it on a single object because we're doing something that requires some concentrated attention, if that's what's happening.
But then the wonderful thing is that we can notice through our mindfulness practice, "oh, I'm done with that task now."
Then we can take that concentration and spread it evenly across all of experience and just be stable and awake and ready for the next thing.
Sometimes concentration has a very narrow connotation, which is unhealthy for us because we just become this thinking-too-hard machine and we never stop, right?
Chronic stress is the result, which is different from awakening.
So lastly, we have the seventh factor, and here I have to admit a mistake.
Because somehow I got on our little sheet wisdom as the seventh factor which is all wrong.
Wisdom is an important mental factor in Buddhism, but in this scheme the seventh factor is actually equanimity.
Somehow I got that mixed up.
And equanimity, let's see, somewhere here I lost track of my notes.
The etymology of equanimity, I can't find it now, but it's something like "grabbed by" or "not caught by."
Equanimity is a quality of a mental factor that has the quality of equal response, or unruffledness.
Equanimity does not mean deadness or not feeling.
It involves fully feeling what's happening, but being able to feel with a little sense of "ah."
Both really good things, "ah, there's a really good thing that I like," and really difficult things, "ah, there's a difficult thing that I don't like, and I can feel the difficulty of that."
Equanimity is a sort of grounding, and of course it's very obviously connected to the factors of calm and concentration.
One way they look at it is that all three of those are a kind of equanimity.
Calm is a quiet equanimity, concentration is a grounded equanimity, and the main equanimity is just equality of response.
So I was thinking, how do we bring this into our life?
It's not so easy, right?
When we're caught, we're caught.
When something happens that upsets us, we are actually upset.
This equanimity practice, this seven factors practice, is not some kind of denial of emotion or suppression of emotion, which we can so easily attempt.
We were looking the other day, I said this last week, I can't remember, in one of the classes at some neurological research on meditation.
Did I talk about this last week?
It turns out that both novice meditators and experienced meditators are able to stay a little calmer in the face of pain in the body or upsetting images.
But the way they're doing it is totally different.

The novice meditators tend to be suppressing the experience of the pain or of the emotion, and the parts of their brains that would normally light up when you're feeling those things don't light up when they put you in the brain scanner.
Experienced meditators, on the other hand, are feeling them more acutely and not evaluating them.
They're not thinking about whether this is good for me or bad for me.
Just feeling them.
So that's interesting.
Maybe there's just an organic progression for us as we study meditation and things like these seven factors.
Naturally, at first, we may use the breath in some way to chill ourselves out, and just like [unclear: "woe be on"].
"I'm just breathing.
I'm not going to think about that."
Then later it becomes more possible, or safer, to just open the heart and say, "Okay, this really hurts."
And I don't have to jump up and fix it right now.
Or I can take this one action, but I see that this other action would probably make it worse, like addictive actions, for instance.
So I was thinking about working with all these factors, and maybe one way to look at it is with three steps.
I'll say a little more about equanimity in a minute, but with all seven factors, the first step might be to build a good foundation.
The second step might be to remember to incline the mind, like we were saying earlier.
To actually bring this up in mind and say, "Wow, I wonder if I can move the mind in that direction, or point it that way."
And the third might be to accept whatever happens.
The good foundation is of course our whole life.
So here we're back to the ethical precepts.
How are we living?
What are the effects of our choices?
Do we habitually make choices that wind us up and make it harder for us to remember to do these practices and work with our mind in this way?
What's our relationship to drugs and alcohol, for instance?
What's our relationship to sleeping enough, if we can sleep enough?
Do we seek support for positive habits like exercise, meditation, eating well and so on?
Do we practice restraint?
So there may be some foundational things we can do that pave the way and make it more possible.
Then inclining the mind, we talked about.

Just to notice, "Wow, I feel really dull and really upset, and I wonder if I can incline my mind towards investigation, towards curiosity right now, towards diligence and energy, even though I don't feel like it.
I'm going to sit down on the cushion."
I was having a conversation with people the other day about resistance to daily practice.
Some of us were saying, "Oh, I'm kind to my resistance and I feel it in the body, and then I walk carefully and I sit down, and that helps me."
Somebody else said, "When my mind is going like that, I tell it shut up.
And that has changed my practice and really helps me."
Good idea.
So there's some skillfulness to inclining the mind.
There's no one way.
And then the third step: we've got to accept the results, right?
Nothing else will work.
Everything else is just a recipe for suffering.
Let's see what else I thought about equanimity.
Oh yes.
A traditional way to set up markers that we can use for equanimity practice, and that are really useful, are the eight worldly concerns.
The eight worldly concerns of Buddhism.
It's a list of the Buddha's, and it was taught specifically to householders.
So this is for us.
To watch out for these eight concerns, not to fall too much into either one of these pairs.
There are four pairs.
The first pair is pleasure and pain.
The second pair is praise and blame.
The third pair is fame and dishonor.
And the fourth pair is gain and loss.
They're all glosses on the same thing, in a way: what we want and what we don't want.
Pleasure and pain, praise and blame, fame and dishonor, gain and loss.
Which sums up our whole society.
It's all about avoiding one and trying to get the other, or being jealous of other people who appear to have the other, which maybe actually they don't from their point of view.
As much as we desire the positive one, and there's nothing wrong with enjoying what we take as positive, these teachings of equanimity suggest that that's a very unstable point of view.
To try to just be praiseworthy, enjoying pleasure, [unclear: "full events"], to have a little fame.
Probably none of us would do it.
I don't want to be really famous.
It would be nice if people around town liked me.
Kind of knew who I was.
Maybe at least at the co-op.
We at least see fame at the co-op.
And it would be really bad to have dishonor and infamy at the co-op, and have everybody avoiding us, and the checkers are like, "I don't even want your member number.
We have a special number for people like you."
So there's nothing wrong with desiring a little praise.
It's wonderful to be praised.
It feels good.
But what the Buddha was saying is you can't hang your hat on it.
It's not stable.
If you're seeking praise and trying to hold on to praise, you put yourself into an off-balance position always.
You can't be steady, and you can't accept what happens.
And of course then it always comes down to life and death.
Ultimately you're not going to accept the inevitable decay and death of yourself and all of your friends, because that doesn't fit into the happy world of praise, fame, gain and pleasure.

So he's suggesting that it's possible to have some middle ground, some stability, where when praise comes you [unclear: "try that"] pleasant feeling, if that's what arises, or the unpleasant feeling if that's what arises, or that attempt to deny and shake off the praise.
You see people doing that.
"No, it's just luck."
People try to dodge praise all the time.
So to be able to just feel it and let it go and accept that outcome, that third step, and also the same with blame.
To accept whatever information is there and not let it stick to you.
Neither praiseworthy nor blameworthy is the Buddhist point of view.
If we really want to be all in for awakening, for this deeper stability, this happiness that's not contingent upon people running around and being nice to us, then we can't be caught either way.
Neither one can hold us that tightly, and we can't hold it that tightly.
So it's a really interesting practice to work with the positive emotions in this way, because it's really hard to work with the negative ones.
That's maybe a little too hard for us.
So I have a suggested practice for us.
The next time you find yourself in a situation where you're receiving praise, you think, "Oh, that never happens."
Well, pay attention.
It probably does.
Guaranteed, actually.
Definitely you get some praise.
See if you can really let that in, really feel it, and then really let go.
It's really inclining the mind through a process, to release from it again.

So the other night, John and Berta and I and several others probably here were at the Checkin' It Radio Hour at Whatcom Community College to see our Sangha friend, and I think she's a member of [unclear: "Red Sooters N2"], yes, Ruth Ozeki, who has written her third novel.
She's a novelist.
It's a really difficult novel to write.
She worked on it for a long, long time.
And it appears it's going to be very successful, like it's going to be a [unclear: "significant American that are at work"].
So she's getting interviewed on NPR and articles in New York.
It turns out the first article in the New York Times was only the initial article, and now there's going to be a long article in the New York Times, maybe the New York Times review of books.
So we went to see Ruth, who was on the Checkin' It Radio Hour program, being interviewed by a professor at Whatcom, and she was perfect.
Charming, engaging, interesting, spontaneous.
It wasn't sort of patlines, like people can do if they have been doing these presentations over and over and over again every night for months, which she has.
She was very down to earth, and we got hugs in the lobby, and it was just lovely.
She seems to be currently on a fame trajectory, getting lots of praise.

And one of the things she said to me that was interesting, she said, "You know what I realized about book tour, which is making this book tour so much more possible than any other book tour I've ever done?
I realized it's just the same as Zen practice.
It's just the same as sesshin, our formal long retreat practice.
I just feel each moment, and I return to the moment, and I let it go, and I just have to stay steady."
Plus, the deal is her publishers are flying her all over creation, which is in the second book.
She was doing this talk in Bellingham on Tuesday night, and then she had an 11 a.m. brunch talk to give in Anaheim, California.
So this involved a 4:30 a.m. flight from SeaTac.
And she's like, "It's just sesshin.
Tough schedule, but you just do it."
Oh, excuse me, I'm going a little bit over.
Is it okay if I spend a few more minutes?
Is everyone okay?
If you need to go, please do.
We're recording it.
I had one more point to make, so it might be about four or five more minutes.
Excuse me for that.
So that was wonderful to see her do that.

Then I realized that the week before I had also had a smaller-scale fame and praise experience, so I just wanted to tell you about that, and suggest this practice of noticing praise and fame, or whatever it is for you.
Really feeling it.
Don't try to deflect it.
Thank the person really sincerely.
Smile.
And then go home and see what it is to release that energy again, to bring up calm, to bring up equanimity.
I was giving a presentation on mindfulness, which I'm doing non-stop lately.
I was invited to the monthly education meeting of the National Association for Mental Illness, which is a wonderful advocacy and education group.
It's been around for a while, from when having a mentally ill child was a serious stigma, so they've set out to fix that, and they've made some progress.
It's a wonderful group.
NAMI, they're called by their initials.
They have a monthly educational forum at a kind of dingy education room at St.
Luke's, and usually, I guess, 15 or 20 people come and learn a few things about depression or anxiety or something.
It's wonderful, but a low-key part of the community.
They really wanted me to come and talk about mindfulness, and they were very excited and did more publicity than usual, and they had many volunteers there.
So instead of 15 or 20 people, there were like 50 people there, and we barely fit in the room.
I really tried to show up and do a good job.
I seemed to really love it, and it was going really well.
I'm finally wrapping it up and ready to rest, and I was putting out energy.
One of the people raised her hand, who had been in one of my classes, and she kind of interrupted me a little bit.
She said, "Before you end, I have to say something.
And that is, everyone here needs to understand what a treasure you are, Tim, and how important it is that you're in Bellingham, and how valuable these classes are.
My husband and I took your shortest class and it has changed our lives and changed our relationship with our daughter.
Nothing is the same and so much better.
So I really needed to say that."
And I'm like, "Thanks.
And refreshments are in the back, and good night."
Then I went home, pretty buzzed, and my wife was on the couch, and "How was the presentation, honey?"
"It was great!"
And then I could see these words kind of, and I'm like, "Whoa."
So I tried to bring up calm and incline the mind towards equanimity.
I tried to do this, and it was interesting.
There was a feeling in the belly of warmth.
I tried to stop and I said, "Hold on a second."
And I went and kind of [unclear: "put it around"] the kitchen to give myself a little cool-down time.
And I could let it go.
What I realized was that when I was in the grips of the excitement of praise and fame, I couldn't really be present at home.
I couldn't really be there.
I was in the middle of being famous.
So I tried to end my 15 minutes and come back to Earth.

I don't know how this would be for you, all of us are different, but it wasn't a matter of suppressing that or denying it, or trying to think of the five things I did wrong in the presentation, which is another thing we do where we try to short-circuit it.
It's not a short-circuiting thing.
It's not a talking ourselves out of something.
I mean, I did do a great job with the presentation.
It was helpful to many of those 50 people.
But it's more just recognizing that energy is there and bringing the mind somewhere else.
Just bringing up calm.
It felt great, actually.
It was like this feeling of something pouring out that was needed, like watering the Earth or something.
Just let that water the Earth.
The Earth will appreciate it.
You'll be the better for it, and ready for the next time you get praise.
Okay.
That's my little talk on equanimity, and I look forward to hearing how it is for you, working with praise and blame, gain and loss.
And these things get very serious.
I'm worried about people's economic lives.
Gain and loss is very real.

And yet there's something about how we hold it, and what our attitude is towards these positive and negative factors of life, that the seven factors really are practical and really can help us to meet life with a little more ease and presence, to where some of these things are going to work out a little better for us.
Okay.
Thanks.

verbatim.text: Well, I was really enjoying tonight how our somewhat elaborate structure just creates so many opportunities, you know. Opportunities to train and to try these different jobs. So I just want to thank everybody who's trying different roles in the zendo.
